title: Stress Dependence of Minimum Creep Rate and Creep Deformation Behavior of Gr.91 and 2.25Cr-1Mo Steels

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Nine to twelve pct Cr tempered martensitic steels can offer the highest potential to meet the required flexibility for thick section boiler and turbine components in ultra-supercritical (USC) power plants with steam temperatures at around 873 K (600 °C), because of their smaller thermal expansion and larger thermal conductivity than austenitic steels and Ni base superalloys. [ 1 ]  At present, 9Cr-1Mo-0.2 V-0.05Nb steel, specified as American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Grade 91 steel, is one of the most popular creep-strength-enhanced-ferritic (CSEF) steels widely used in boiler components of USC power plants. 2.25Cr-1Mo steel, of which creep strength is lower than Gr. 91 steel, is widely used in boiler components of power plants with steam temperatures at around 823 K (550 °C).

In many cases, there is substantially no steady-state stage in engineering creep resistant steels and alloys, where the tertiary or accelerating creep stage begins immediately after the primary or transient creep stage and the creep life consists of the primary or transient and tertiary or accelerating regions. [ 4 ]  Therefore, the term “minimum creep rate” has been favored by engineers and researchers who are concerned with engineering creep resistant steels and alloys.

The purpose of the present research is to investigate for Gr.91 and 2.25Cr-1Mo steels the relationship between the stress dependence of the minimum creep rate and the creep deformation behavior in the transition region, paying particular attention to microstructure evolution and uniform or localized deformation.

sections.heading: Creep Data and Analytical Procedure
paragraphs: The creep data for Gr.91 steel examined were those for the three heats MGA, MGB and MGC of tube materials and those for the three heats MgA, MgB and MgC of plate materials in the NIMS Creep Data Sheet No. 43A [ 12 ]  and Atlas of Creep Deformation Property Nos. D1 and D2. [ 13 , 14 ]  The maximum time to rupture  t r  was 1.1 × 10 5  h. The name of heat such as MGA is due to the reference code in the NIMS Creep Data Sheets. The Atlas of Creep Deformation Property contains many graphs showing creep curves, creep rate  vs  time curves and creep rate  vs  strain curves over wide temperature and stress ranges, together with the chemical compositions and heat treatment conditions of the respective heats. The present Gr.91 steel was subjected to normalizing at around 1050 °C and then to tempering at around 760 °C. Creep specimens of 6 mm diameter and 30 mm gauge length were taken from the Gr.91 steel tubes, while those of 10 mm diameter and 50 mm gauge length were taken from the Gr.91 steel plates.

After tempering, the present steel was observed to be tempered martensitic microstructure, having prior austenite grain size of about 10  µ m, where high-density dislocations, fine M 23 C 6  carbides and fine MX carbo-nitrides were distributed.  [ 15 ]  A prior austenite grain consisted of several packets and each packet consisted of many laths. The distribution of dislocations was not homogeneous after tempering, such as that some laths contained high-density dislocations but that some laths contained low-density dislocations. Even in a lath, the distribution of dislocations was not homogeneous. The dislocations had intricately tangled each other, forming complex dislocation structure. The M in the M 23 C 6  carbides was mainly Cr. The M in the MX carbo-nitrides was V and Nb and the X was carbon and nitrogen. The M 23 C 6  carbides were mainly distributed along lath, packet and prior austenite grain boundaries, while the MX carbo-nitrides were mainly distributed in the matrix. The size of M 23 C 6  carbides along prior austenite grain boundaries was larger than that along lath and packet boundaries inside grains.

The creep data for 2.25Cr-1Mo steel examined were those for the heat MAF of tube material, specified as Japanese Industrial Standard (JIS) Steel Tube Boiler Alloy (STBA) 24, and those for the heat MnG of plate material, specified as American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) A542/A542M, in the NIMS Creep Data Sheet No. 3B [ 16 ]  and No. 36B, [ 17 ]  respectively. The tubes of JIS STBA 24 were subjected to heat treatment of annealing, which consisted of 20 minutes at 930 °C, then cooled to 720 °C and 130 minutes at 720 °C followed by air cooling. The plates of ASTM A542/A542M were subjected to quenching and tempering, which consisted of 6 hours at 930 °C followed by water quenching, then 6 hours at 635 °C followed by air cooling and 2 hours at 600 °C followed by furnace cooling. The microstructure after heat treatment consisted of ferrite and pearlite containing M 23 C 6  and Mo 2 C carbides for the JIS STBA 24, while that was tempered martensite containing high density of dislocations and carbides for the ASTM A542/A542M. The chemical compositions are given in the NIMS Creep Data Sheets. [ 16 , 17 ]  The creep data for long-term-serviced material of JIS STBA 24, [ 18 , 19 ]  which had already been exposed at 577 °C and 34 MPa for 194,958 hours as a superheater tube in a commercial plant, were also examined. The two materials of JIS STBA 24 are called the virgin and long-term serviced materials in this paper, according to their history. Although the dislocation density in the virgin material of JIS STBA 24 was rather low after heat treatment because of ferrite/pearlite microstructure, the dislocation density was further decreased during the long-term-service.

sections.heading: Creep Rupture Data and Minimum Creep Rate of Gr.91 Steel
paragraphs: Figure  2  shows the creep rupture data for the six heats of Gr.91 steel at 823 K (550 °C), 873 K (600 °C) and 923 K (650 °C). The degradation in creep rupture strength becomes more significant with decreasing stress and with increasing test duration, as shown by the increasing slope of stress  vs  time to rupture curves with decreasing stress and with increasing test duration. The heats MgA and MgB shown by the solid symbols exhibit lower creep rupture strength than the other heats from short-times to long-times. Fig. 2 Creep rupture data for six heats of Gr.91 at 823 (550), 873 (600) and 923 K (650 °C). The gray line shows a boundary between large and low values of stress exponent  n 1  of minimum creep rate

The present author showed for Gr.91 steel that the time to rupture  t r  at high stresses and short times exhibited a monotonous increase with increasing 0.2 pct proof stress at the creep test temperatures. [ 20 ]  The 0.2 pct proof stress, corresponding to the initial strength of the heats at the creep test temperature, depends on temperature and time conditions of normalizing and tempering heat treatments. The heat treatment conditions of Gr.91 steel examined are given in Table  I . The 0.2 pct proof stress basically decreases with increasing mean diffusion distance of iron during tempering heat treatment. [ 20 ]  The annealing time of 10 minutes in the normalizing for the heat MgB may be too short to fully re-dissolve MX carbonitrides, indicating that a large number of undissolved MX carbonitrides with a large size remain and hence that the concentration of MX-forming elements, such as dissolved V and Nb in the matrix, is rather low after normalizing and before tempering. This causes that the precipitation of fine MX carbonitrides during tempering is only a little bit, resulting in a low value of 0.2 pct proof stress. Table I Heat Treatment Conditions of Gr.91 Steel Examined Heat Normalizing Tempering MGA 1045 °C/10 min AC 780 °C/60 min AC MGB 1050 °C/60 min AC 760 °C/60 min AC MGC 1050 °C/10 min AC 765 °C/30 min AC MgA 1050 °C/10 min AC 770 °C/60 min AC, 740 °C/8.4 h FC MgB 1050 °C/10 min AC 770 °C/60 min AC, 740 °C/60 min FC MgC 1060 °C/90 min AC 760 °C/60 min AC, 730 °C/8.4 h FC

The gray line in Figure  2  drawn across the creep rupture data at three temperatures shows a boundary between the large values of  n 1  ≳ 10 and small values of  n 1  ≈ 4 to 7. The change in the value of  n 1  from large values of  n 1  ≳ 10 to small values of  n 1  ≈ 4 to 7 reflects the difference in creep deformation behavior between high-stress and short-time conditions and low-stress and long-time conditions.

sections.heading: Creep Deformation Behavior of Gr.91 Steel in Transient Region
paragraphs: Figure  4  shows the creep rate  vs  time curves and creep rate  vs  strain curves of the heat MGC of Gr.91 steel at 873 K (600 °C), [ 13 ]  where the arrows show the time to minimum creep rate  t m  and strain to minimum creep rate  ε m . The  t m  increases with decreasing stress, while the  ε m  is constant of 2.2 pct at high stresses of 160 to 140 MPa and decreases with decreasing stress below 140 MPa at 873 K (600 °C). The change in  t m  in the stress range between 160 and 70 MPa is more than two orders of magnitude, which is much larger than that in  ε m , smaller than one order of magnitude. Fig. 4 ( a ) creep rate  vs  time curves and ( b ) creep rate  vs  strain curves of heat MGC of Gr.91 steel at 873 K (600 °C). The arrows show time to minimum creep rate  t m  and strain to minimum creep rate  ε m

Kushima  et al. [ 15 ]  observed a decrease in dislocation density in the present Gr.91 steel during creep at 873 K (600 °C) and 100 to 160 MPa, indicating the movement and annihilation of dislocations contribute to the creep deformation. They also observed that the hardness decreased with increasing creep rupture test duration at 873 (600), 923 (650) and 973 K (700 °C). The appearance of transient creep region in Figure  4  and the movement and annihilation of dislocations during creep suggest that the creep deformation in the present Gr.91 steel is due to the mechanism of dislocation creep.

The present author has revealed for tempered martensitic 9Cr steel that the transient creep is basically a consequence of the movement and annihilation of a high density of dislocations due to martensitic microstructure and that the accelerating creep is a consequence of gradual loss of creep strength due to the microstructure recovery, such as the agglomeration of carbides and the growth of martensite lath subgrains. [ 21 ]  The V-shaped creep-rate curves in Figure  4  are considered to result from an overlapping of the two creep-rate curves, one of which is a consequence of the movement and annihilation of excess dislocations in the transient region and the other of which is a consequence of a gradual loss of creep strength due to microstructural evolution in the accelerating region, as shown in Figure  6 . The effect of creep strength loss is pronounced after the decrease in creep rate due to dislocation annihilation occurring sufficiently. Fig. 6 Schematic creep rate  vs  time curve

The mechanisms of appearance of minimum creep rate are closely correlated with the microstructure recovery. The coarsening of laths with absorbing excess dislocations is the major process in the acceleration creep of tempered martensitic 9Cr steel. [ 21 ]  The present authors suggested that the progressive local-coalescence of two adjacent lath boundaries near the Y-junction causes the movement of Y-junction, resulting in the coarsening of laths. [ 22 ]  It should be noted that the M 23 C 6  carbides are distributed along lath boundaries after tempering and during creep and that the M 23 C 6  carbides exert pinning force on moving lath boundaries. Thus, the creep deformation in the tempered martensitic 9Cr steel involves complicated processes but not a simple process where dislocations merely overcome precipitate particles as proposed by Ansel and Weertman. [ 7 ]  This is a reason why the stress exponent of the minimum creep rate of Gr.91 steel exhibits large values of 10 or more at high stress region. The derivation of a creep rate equation with large stress exponent of 10 or more based on appropriate modelling has not been achieved.

Figure  7 (a) schematically shows the creep stress and distribution of obstacle strength inside grain and in the vicinity of prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs). At a stress  σ 1 , which is higher than the strength of all the obstacles at a time  t 1 , the creep deformation takes place as dislocations easily overcome all the obstacles, corresponding to the homogeneous deformation throughout the specimen. The onset of accelerating creep takes place when the creep strain reaches 2.2 pct as shown in Figures  4 (b) and  5 (c). At a stress  σ 2 , which is lower than  σ 1  but higher than the strength of parts of obstacles at time  t 2 , the creep deformation is localized in the area, where the stress  σ 2  is higher than the strength of obstacles. The time  t 2  is larger than  t 1  because of  σ 2  <   σ 1 . The strength of the obstacles decreases with increasing test duration by microstructure recovery during creeps, which is more significant in the vicinity of PAGB, because the coarsening of precipitates and the recovery of martensitic microstructure are enhanced by grain boundary diffusion. Kushima  et al.  observed that the recovery of martensitic microstructure was localized in the vicinity of PAGBs in the heat MGC of the present Gr.91 steel after creep rupture testing for 34,141 hours at 600 °C and 100 MPa. [ 20 ]  At a stress  σ 3 , which is lower than  σ 2 , the creep deformation is more localized in the vicinity of PAGBs than that at  σ 2 . This indicates that the  ε m  decreases with decreasing stress and hence that the localization of creep deformation becomes more significant with decreasing stress. Fig. 7 Schematics of creep stress and distributions of obstacle strength inside grain and near prior austenite grain boundary. ( a ) influence of creep stress and test duration and ( b ) influence of strong and weak heats

Figure  7 (b) schematically compares the localization of creep deformation between strong and weak heats. At a high stress  σ 1 , the creep deformation takes place in both the strong and weak heats as dislocations easily overcome all the obstacles. When the strain reaches 2.2 pct, the onset of accelerating creep takes place in both the strong and weak heats, as shown in Figure  5 (c). At a stress  σ 2 , the creep deformation is localized in the vicinity of PAGBs of the strong heat, while the creep deformation still takes place homogeneously throughout the specimen of the weak heat as the  σ 2  is larger than the obstacle strength in the weak heat. The localization of creep deformation is more significant in the strong heat than in the weak heat, as can be seen from Figure  5 (c).

The coarsening of laths with absorbing excess dislocations takes place during creep , [ 15 ]  although details of dislocation structure are not clear in the present research. The M 23 C 6  carbides are distributed along lath boundaries after tempering and during creep and the M 23 C 6  carbides exert pinning force on moving lath boundaries. The present author suggested that the progressive local coalescence of two adjacent lath boundaries near the Y-junction causes the movement of Y-junction, resulting in the coarsening of laths. [ 22 ]  The dislocation structure should be clearly studied in future to understand the mechanisms responsible for the creep deformation.

sections.heading: Reduction of Stress Exponent n 1  for Minimum Creep Rate of Gr.91 Steel
Apparent Activation Energy for Minimum Creep Rate of Gr.91 Steel
Stress Dependence and Apparent Activation Energy for Minimum Creep Rate of 2.25Cr-1Mo Steel
paragraphs: Figure  9  shows the creep rupture data for 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as JIS STBA 24 with ferrite/pearlite microstructure containing low dislocation density and those for 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as ASTM A542/A542M with tempered martensitic microstructure containing high dislocation density at 823 K (550 °C). [ 16 , 17 ]  The creep rupture strength is larger in the ASTM A542/A542M than in the JIS STBA 24 at short times less than about 10,000 hours, presumably due to higher dislocation density in the ASTM A542/A542M than in the JIS STBA 24 after heat treatment. The 0.2 pct proof stress measured by tensile test was 192 to 253 MPa for the twelve heats of JIS STBA 24 at 823 K (550 °C), which was much lower than that of 378 to 464 MPa for the seven heats of ASTM A542/A542M at 823 K (550 °C). [ 16 , 17 ]  The degradation in creep rupture strength is more significant in the ASTM A542/A542M than in the JIS STBA 24 at long times above about 10,000 hours. The creep rupture strength of the JIS STBA 24 and ASTM A542/A542M reverses after more than 50,000 hours. Kushima  et al.  observed that the decrease in hardness of the creep ruptured specimens with increasing test duration was more significant in the ASTM A542/A542M than in the JIS STBA 24 at 723 (450) to 923 K (650 °C). [ 23 ]  This indicats the recovery of dislocations during creep is more significant in the ASTM A542/A542M than in the JIS STBA 24. Higher dislocation density in the ASTM A542/A542M than in the JIS STBA 24 promotes the recovery of dislocations with the aid of stress during creep. Fig. 9 Creep rupture data for twelve heats of 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as JIS STBA 24 and for seven heats of 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as ASTM A542/A542M at 823 K (550 °C)

Figure  11  shows the creep rate  vs  time curves and creep rate  vs  strain curves of the virgin material of JIS STBA 24 at 823 K (550 °C), while Figure  12  shows those of the long-term serviced material at 850 K (577 °C). [ 18 ]  The  t m  increases with decreasing stress, while the  ε m  is approximately constant of 3.0 and 5.5 pct for the virgin and long-term serviced materials, respectively, in the stress range examined. The constant  ε m  suggests that the creep deformation is homogeneous but not localized in both the virgin and long-term serviced materials of JIS STBA 24 in the stress range examined. Fig. 11 ( a ) creep rate  vs  time curves and ( b ) creep rate  vs  strain curves of virgin material of heat MAF of 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as JIS STBA 24 at 823 K (550 °C). The arrows show time to minimum creep rate  t m  and strain to minimum creep rate  ε m Fig. 12 ( a ) creep rate  vs  time curves and ( b ) creep rate  vs  strain curves of long-term serviced material of 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as JIS STBA 24 at 850 K (577 °C). The arrows show time to minimum creep rate  t m  and strain to minimum creep rate  ε m

Ohba  et al.  observed the TEM microstructure of the long-term serviced material of STBA 24 after interrupting the creep test at 577 °C and 69 MPa for 1008 hours, which corresponded to a time to minimum creep rate. [ 19 ]  They observed that dynamic recovery or recrystallisation took place during transient creep, resulting in the formation of subgrains where the density of dislocations and carbides was very low. They pointed out that the formation of subgrains causes a decrease in resistance to creep deformation and promotes the onset of accelerating creep. The carbides, such as M 23 C 6  and Mo 2 C, exert pinning force on moving subgrain boundaries. Thus, the creep deformation in the present 2.25Cr-1Mo steel involves complicated processes, such as the movement of subgrain boundaries pinned by the carbides, but not a simple process where dislocations merely overcome the precipitate particles as proposed by Ansel and Weertman. [ 7 ]  The complicated creep deformation is a reason why the stress exponent of the minimum creep rate of JIS STBA 24 exhibits large values of 10 to 11. This is similar as the situation in Gr.91 steel described in the Section  III–D .

The ASTM A542/A542M with tempered martensitic microstructure exhibits the reduction of the  n 1  from a large value of  n 1  = 11 in the high stress region to a small value of  n 1  = 4 in the low stress region in Figure  10 . This is similar as the reduction of  n 1  in Gr.91 steel with tempered martensitic microstructure. Unfortunately we have no data on creep rate  vs  time curves and creep rate  vs  strain curves and hence we have no data on  t m  and  ε m  for the ASTM A542/A542M. The reduction of  n 1  from a large value of  n 1  = 11 to a small value of  n 1  = 4 is considered to be due to a change in creep deformation from homogeneous to localized mode, similar as Gr.91 steel. In the JIS STBA 24 steel with ferrite/pearlite microstructure, the low dislocation density results in a reduced driving force for dislocation recovery in the vicinity of PAGBs, allowing homogeneous creep deformation to persist for up to low stresses.

sections.heading: Virtual Minimum Creep Rate of Gr.91 Steel Assuming Homogeneous Deformation in Transient Region
Microstructural Features for Localized Creep Deformation
paragraphs: Figure  18  shows schematically the different microstructural features in Gr.91 steel during creep. During creep at high-stress and short-time conditions, at 873 K (600 °C) and 200 to 120 MPa, the coarsening of laths with absorbing excess dislocations takes place homogeneously through inside grains and near PAGBs. At low-stress and long-time conditions, at 873 K (600 °C) and 120 to 70 MPa, the localized microstructure recovery takes place near PAGBs. The recovery of excess dislocations near PAGBs is enhanced by grain boundary diffusion. The recovery of dislocations enhances the coarsening of M 23 C 6  carbides and laths. Coarsening of laths produces subgrains with low density dislocations inside subgrain and sparce M 23 C 6  carbides at subgrain boundaries. A high dislocation density results in a large driving force for dislocation recovery. Therefore, the high dislocation density in tempered martensitic microstructure is an important feature for the localized creep deformation near PAGBs at low-stress and long-time conditions. This is the same situation in 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as ASTM A542/A542M with tempered martensitic microstructure. In 2.25Cr-1Mo steel specified as JIS STBA 24 with ferrite/pearlite microstructure, on the other hand, the localized creep deformation near PAGBs is unlikely to take place due to low dislocation density. Fig. 18 Schematics of microstructure of Gr.91 steel after tempering and after creep for a time to reach minimum creep rate. ( a ) after tempering, ( b ) after creep at high-stress and short-time conditions, showing homogeneous microstructure evolution and ( c ) after creep at low-stress and long-time conditions, showing localized microstructure recovery near PAGBs. The areas shaded in gray color indicate regions where high-density dislocations are distributed
